summary: Trinidad and Tobago is a twin-island country at the southern end of the Caribbean, known for its oil and natural gas industry, Carnival, calypso and steelpan music.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Britain seized Trinidad in 1797 and acquired Tobago in 1814, bringing Protestant denominations such as the Anglican, Methodist and Moravian churches. In 1868 Canadian Presbyterian missionaries began preaching among the Indian indentured laborers and running schools, drawing some Indo-Trinidadians to convert. In recent years Pentecostalism has grown rapidly; the Afro-Caribbean Spiritual Baptists were banned by the colonial government by law from 1917 to 1951 and now have a national holiday of their own.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Trinidad was a Spanish colony before 1797, and in 1783 Spain issued the Cédula de Población, inviting Catholic French plantation owners and their slaves to settle, which put down roots for Catholicism on the island. After the British takeover Catholicism remained the main faith of the Afro-Creoles and French-descended families, and it is still the largest single denomination.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: After abolition in 1834 the plantations lacked labor, and in 1845 the first ship carrying Indian indentured laborers, the Fatel Razack, arrived; by 1917 about 140,000 Indians had come to Trinidad, most of them Hindus. Their descendants today make up more than a third of the population, Divali is a national holiday, and May 30 each year is also designated Indian Arrival Day.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Muslims are mainly descendants of the Muslims among the Indian indentured laborers, and in the early colonial period some of the African slaves brought over also followed Islam. The Hosay festival of the Islamic month of Muharram derives from the Shia ritual commemorating Husayn and has developed in Trinidad into a procession in which many ethnic groups take part. In 1990 the radical group Jamaat al Muslimeen launched an attempted coup.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Trinidad and Tobago is a society with a strong religious atmosphere; Christian, Hindu and Islamic festivals are all national holidays, and religious activity is closely tied to community life. Very few people therefore say they have no religion, and they are mainly young people influenced by secularization in cities such as the capital, Port of Spain.

religion.background: The indigenous people of Trinidad almost disappeared after Spanish colonization, and in the late 18th century French Catholic plantation owners and African slaves moved in in large numbers, laying down the Catholic tradition. After the British takeover in 1797 various Protestant denominations arrived, and Afro-Caribbeans developed the Spiritual Baptist faith and Orisha belief, blending West African beliefs. The Indian indentured laborers of 1845–1917 brought Hinduism and Islam. Today the festivals of every religion are national holidays, and Trinidad and Tobago is often seen as representative of Caribbean religious diversity.

ranking.name: English (including Trinidadian English Creole)
ranking.description: After Britain took Trinidad in 1797, English gradually became the language of administration and education, replacing the Spanish and French Creole that had been in common use in the early colonial period. The everyday spoken language is Trinidadian English Creole, which blends vocabulary from West African languages, French, Spanish and Hindi. Because schools, the media and the government use English throughout, almost all citizens have English or an English-based creole as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Trinidadian Hindustani
ranking.description: Trinidadian Hindustani derives from the Bhojpuri and Awadhi spoken by the Indian indentured laborers of 1845–1917. After English education spread in the 20th century, Indo-Trinidadian families gradually switched to English, and today fluent speakers are mostly elderly, but many words survive in food names, religious rituals and "chutney" music.

language.history: The indigenous people of Trinidad spoke Arawak and Carib, and during the Spanish colonial period Spanish was the official language. At the end of the 18th century large numbers of French plantation owners moved in, and French Creole became the most widely spoken language on the island in the 19th century. After British rule English-language education was promoted, and in the 20th century English and English Creole replaced French Creole. The Hindustani brought by the Indian indentured laborers gradually declined but left a large number of loanwords.

ranking.name: Doubles
ranking.description: Two soft, puffy fried flatbreads called "bara" are filled with curried chickpeas and topped with tamarind sauce, mango chutney and pepper sauce, the most popular breakfast street snack.
ranking.history: Doubles originated in the food traditions of the Indian indentured laborers and is generally believed to have begun in 1936 when the Indo-Trinidadian vendor Emamool Deen began selling curried chickpeas in bread in Princes Town in southern Trinidad. Customers reportedly often asked for the bread to be "doubled," giving rise to the name "doubles." Today it is the most representative breakfast of Trinidadians, sold in large numbers by street vendors every morning, and has become a symbol of Trinidad's national food.

ranking.name: Roti
ranking.description: A thin flatbread with yellow split pea flour inside, or a layered flatbread torn into pieces, wrapped around or served with curried chicken, goat, potato and chickpeas.
ranking.history: Roti was brought by the Indian indentured laborers who arrived in Trinidad after 1845 and was originally a North Indian everyday flatbread. It is said that in the 1940s an Indo-Trinidadian woman in San Fernando in the south began wrapping curry inside roti to sell, so workers could carry it conveniently, and it has since become a popular takeaway food. The torn layered bread is jokingly called "buss-up shut" (busted shirt), a national food Trinidadians love to eat both daily and at festivals.

ranking.name: Callaloo
ranking.description: Taro leaves (dasheen bush), okra and pumpkin are stewed with coconut milk, onion and spices and blended into a thick green soup, sometimes with crab or salted pork added.
ranking.history: Callaloo comes from the cooking traditions of West African slaves; okra and leafy-vegetable stews are very common in West Africa and, carried to the Caribbean, blended with local produce. In Trinidad it is traditionally a fixture of Sunday lunch, eaten with rice, macaroni pie and stewed chicken. Because it cooks many ingredients together in one pot, Trinidadians also often use "callaloo" as a metaphor for their diverse, blended society.

ranking.name: Pelau
ranking.description: Sugar is first cooked in a pot into caramel and the chicken is browned in it, then rice, pigeon peas and coconut milk are added and simmered together, savory, sweet and rich.
ranking.history: The name and method of pelau derive from the Middle Eastern and Indian "pilaf," brought to Trinidad by Indian indentured laborers, while the technique of burning sugar to color the meat is thought to come from Afro-Caribbean cooking traditions, and the two blended in Trinidad. This one-pot dish is easy to carry and is one of the most common dishes at beach picnics, river outings and festival parties.

ranking.name: Shark and bake
ranking.description: Shark meat is marinated, coated in flour and fried, then put into a soft fried bread called "bake," and diners add toppings such as lettuce, tomato, pineapple, tamarind sauce and garlic sauce themselves.
ranking.history: This snack is inseparable from Maracas Bay on the north coast of Trinidad; from the mid-20th century local fishing families sold it beside the beach, and it later became a food visitors must try. The fried bread "bake" comes from colonial-era bread traditions, and the various sauces reflect the blend of Indian, African and European food. In recent years, because of shark conservation concerns, some shops have also switched to other fish in place of shark.
